Reproduce {{asm}} as source that builds to byte-exact matching asm; never hand-edit the asm. Write {{c}} (K&R C for the Manx Aztec `cc`{{cstyle}}) only if `cc` could have generated this code; otherwise write {{s}} (Manx `as` assembly{{style}}).{{hand}}

Deciding the form. This binary's `cc` flags: {{flags}}. `make info`'s `tool` line shows them too; an `unrecorded` tool means no source exists yet, not that the code is C.
- `cc` output looks like: a prologue on every routine, `mov ax,-N` / `call aztec_csav` under `+b` (N = local frame size, 0 with no locals), `push bp` / `mov bp,sp` without it; arguments at `[bp+4]`, `[bp+6]`, ...; arguments pushed right to left and popped after the call (`pop cx`, `add sp,n`); `cbw` / `sub ah,ah` widening; `push ax` ... `pop ax` temporaries; `jne x` / `jmp near y` pairs and other unoptimized branches; only `si`/`di` kept across a call.
- Hand-written looks like: no prologue at all under `+b`, or the body runs in its caller's frame; arguments or results in registers (a call with no push/pop around it); a value in `ax`-`dx` still used after a `call`; a counter in a register `register` cannot get; `in`/`out`, `cli`/`sti`, `pushf`/`popf`, `int`; segment-register juggling (`push cs; pop ds`); `cld` and string ops; code-segment data; padding `nop`s, or jumps `cc` would shorten; falling through into the next routine (`make info`'s `next` line names it).
One clear hand-written sign outweighs a C-like shape: `cc` never emits port I/O or register-passed arguments.

A .s: `include lmacros.h`, the project's, built from `disassembler/lib/aztec/lmacros_master.h`, which lists each macro's exact expansion. Use its structured blocks `.if`/`.elseif`/`.else`/`.endif`, `.while`/`.endw`, `.repeat`/`.until`, `.break`/`.continue` in place of labels and jumps (conditions `ax == 5`, `al lt 3`, `cx sge 1` (signed), `dl and 2`, `carry?`, `not cx`; no `!`, `<`, `>`). Then use the call, push/pop, clamp, `procdef`/`pret`, `movseg`, `outp`, `fatal` and `jnear` shorthands; write out a custom prologue/epilogue, and use plain instructions where no macro fits. Indent each block body one tab past its directive. Spell routines in `public`, `proc` and `extrn` the way C sees them, `NAME_` (the build drops one trailing `_`); data takes no `_` (`extrn play_device:byte`).

A .c: locals are laid out in declaration order from `bp-2` down, with an array's element 0 at its lowest address, so the frame size and offsets give you the declarations. K&R has no initialized auto arrays: write the stores out. Signedness shows in the code: `cbw` / `jl` mean signed, `sub ah,ah` / `jb` mean unsigned. An `extern` may take any type that gives the same addressing; prefer the shared struct views in `src_DSAVANT/include/structs/`. Don't write layout-dependent C, which hard-codes the data layout instead of declaring it. That means raw byte offsets (`p[415]`, `*(int *)(rec + 6)`), hand-scaled indexes (`t[b * 90 + c * 30 + i * 3 + 1]`), casts used to pick a field's width or sign, and reaching into a neighbouring field (`ranges[t * 4 - 1]`). Declare the layout instead: a struct for each record (fields at their offsets, `pad` arrays for the gaps, a comment with each known field's offset), real multi-dimensional arrays, and pointers typed to the struct (`struct member_rec *party_char[]`). A struct only this .c uses may stay in it. A record that another .c also declares, or that a header under `src_DSAVANT/include/structs/` already describes, goes in that header (an 8.3 name), pulled in with `#include "structs/member.h"`: extend the existing header rather than declaring a second copy, so each layout stays in a single place. The build writes `src_DSAVANT/include/structs.inc` from the original code: one `struc` per record it found, with the field offsets the code actually uses (`.f_0026`, or the names given in the sidecar's `data_names` `record`). Use it as the layout to start from: match its stride and field offsets in the C view, and name the record and its fields in that sidecar `record` so the asm spells them too (`slot_rec.target`). `extern` declarations stay in the .c. Then write `party_char[m]->slot`, `table[b][c][i].target`. Aztec folds field offsets into the same `[bx + label+off]` displacement, so this costs no bytes; keep each expression's shape and operand order. When several labels sit at fixed offsets inside one record (`rec_count` at +4 from `rec_first`), they are a single struct. Name the base in the sidecar with a `record` giving its `size` and `count` (so addresses inside the array spell as its fields), drop the field labels, and convert every .c that used them. Never put a whole routine body in `#asm`: that is what a .s is for, and labels in `#asm` become linker symbols. `#asm` is only for a few instructions inside real C.

Commands (repo root):
- `make probe {{project}} {{binary}} {{label}}` compiles your source with the routine's exact tool and flags and prints its code, length and fixups; use it to iterate on codegen.
- `make rebuild {{project}} {{binary}} {{label}}` gates one routine against the original bytes (for a routine under shared/, `make rebuild {{project}} {{label}}` gates it against every binary that contains it). `make rebuild` alone recompiles every .c/.s and is the final pass/fail gate.
- `make refs {{project}} {{binary}} {{label}}` lists the address-named and content-tagged symbols the routine references. Already-named callees are omitted; declare them `extrn`/`extern` yourself. A dotted shared alias (`stem.bss1`) can't be spelled in C: spell one donor's own name (`bss_95f4`), even when the address falls inside a named array (spelling it as the element, `slot_value[2]`, makes the copies' asm differ). In step 3, name it by the dotted alias (`{{label}}.bss1=NAME`), which names every donor's address at once.
- `make name {{project}} {{binary}} SYMBOL=NAME[:NOTE] ...` writes the sidecar, renames the hand-written sources and every reference in them (file, routine, `NAME_` in .s, `extern`/`extrn`, C callers), then builds and rebuilds. Give SYMBOL as the build spells it (`cseg_0d3a`, `bss_1234`, `io_loc_KRUO`, `{{label}}`) or by its current name, and single-quote any spec whose note has spaces.
- `make build {{project}}` regenerates the asm from the disassembly and sources. The sidecar ({{sidecar}}) and the tooling under disassembler/ are there to read when you need them.

Steps:
1. Write the source with the routine still named `{{label}}`. Iterate with `make probe`, then run `make rebuild {{project}} {{binary}} {{label}}` until it passes. If the only differences left are symbol or label names on the same instructions and offsets, the bytes match: go on to step 2 (step 3's `make name` regenerates the asm). A report that the source compiles to a different size than its fragment means the bytes do not match yet.
2. Give parameters and locals descriptive names in the source itself (C names; `equ` names for .s and #asm stack arguments and locals). Add terse comments that say why, not what: a one-line header above the routine (a `;` line in a .s, `/* */` in C, never `//`), and short trailing comments on loops, branches and magic numbers (BIOS/DOS function numbers, port numbers, key codes, header offsets, strides, flag bits). Describe only what the code shows; don't guess intent.
3. Run `make refs {{project}} {{binary}} {{label}}`, then name everything in one call: `make name {{project}} {{binary}} {{label}}=NAME:'note' SYMBOL=NAME:'note' ...`. NAME for the routine is a descriptive lowercase_underscore name keeping any prefix its flags need. Add every symbol `make refs` listed (globals, code-segment data, called routines, including those only in `extrn` lines) except "label inside" rows, each with a note saying what it holds or does.
4. If `make name` reports a rebuild failure, fix the source and run `make rebuild` until it passes. No address-named or content-tagged symbol may remain in the source, and no layout-dependent C may remain in a .c. Finish with a full `make rebuild`.

Your final message: only the routine's new name, or, if you could not finish, what is left and why.

{{guide}}
